chapter_name: The Theory of the Firm under Perfect Competition
learning_objective: 🎯 Understand how a firm makes profit-maximizing decisions in an ideal, perfectly competitive market where it has no control over the price.

main_concepts.simple_explanation: A market with very large numbers of buyers and sellers, selling homogeneous (identical) products, with free entry and exit, and perfect knowledge. Because products are identical, no single seller can influence the price.

main_concepts.concept_title: 🏷️ The Firm as a Price Taker
main_concepts.simple_explanation: In perfect competition, the market (industry) determines the price based on total demand and supply. The individual firm must accept this price. Therefore, Price = Average Revenue (AR) = Marginal Revenue (MR).
To maximize profit, a firm must produce at the output level where two conditions are met: 1) Marginal Revenue equals Marginal Cost (MR = MC), and 2) MC must be rising at that point.
In the short run, a perfectly competitive firm's supply curve is the upward-sloping portion of its Marginal Cost (MC) curve that lies above the minimum of the Average Variable Cost (AVC) curve.

fun_activity.title: 🌾 The Wheat Farmer
fun_activity.instructions: Imagine you grow wheat. Your wheat is exactly the same as 10,000 other farmers' wheat. If the market price is ₹2,000/quintal, and you try to sell yours for ₹2,001, you will sell zero! Buyers will just go to the farmer next door. You are a true 'Price Taker'.

exam_tips: 📌 Always remember: Under perfect competition, the Demand Curve for the firm is a perfectly elastic horizontal line (AR = MR).
📌 The 'Shut-down Point' occurs when Price falls below the minimum of Average Variable Cost (AVC). If the firm can't even cover its variable costs, it should close.
📌 Normal profit is included in total cost. So when TR = TC, the firm is earning zero 'economic' profit, but it is still earning 'normal' profit!
quick_recap: ⭐ The short-run supply curve of the firm is derived from its Marginal Cost curve.
⭐ Free entry and exit ensure that in the long run, all firms in a perfectly competitive market earn only normal profits.
